topic: WorkOS AI Agent Building Blocks Guide 2026: Tools, MCP Servers, Skills, Orchestrators, and Auth

competitors.title: The building blocks of an AI agent (WorkOS Blog, Jun 2, 2026)
key_points: Five-layer AI agent stack: User/app surface, Agent framework, Tools & MCP servers, LLM/model, Auth & identity
Auth runs through all layers — not a feature added at the end
Agent framework concerns: orchestrator (decision loop), memory (short-term context window + long-term external), system prompt (job description), skills (composable capability bundles)
Tools are functions the LLM can call — defined by name, description, and JSON input schema
MCP standardizes tool exposure over a network — versioned, shared, independently deployable
Skills are packaged reusable agent capabilities: tools + system prompt fragment + context — composable across providers
Session-scoped authorization: agent gets access for task duration only, not indefinitely
Agent as principal: agents need their own identity, client ID, and permission set — distinct from the user
Prompt injection is OWASP's top LLM threat — mitigations are architectural, not model-level

competitors.title: The 2026 AI agent auth checklist: 9 things to audit before you ship (WorkOS Blog, Jun 10, 2026)
key_points: Every agent must have its own identity (OAuth client with own client ID)
Intersection rule: agent permissions = agent role ∩ user permissions, never the union
OIDC for human auth, OAuth 2.1 for delegated authorization — keep strictly separate
Access tokens must be short-lived (5-30 min), audience-bound, and scoped to the task
Sensitive actions require explicit human approval (HITL pattern)
Tokens vaulted server-side, never in agent process or model context
Immutable audit log with 5 questions: who initiated, which agent, what data, what result, why permitted
Immediate revocation per agent and per user
Fail closed: 401 means halt, never retry with different credentials

competitors.title: Delegated access for AI agents: The intersection rule explained (WorkOS Blog, Jun 10, 2026)
key_points: Run-as-user pattern collapses two relationships: what user can do vs what agent should do on user's behalf
OWASP LLM06 (excessive agency) is one of the most exploited vulnerability classes in production agent systems
Two access models: application-wide (service account, broad access) vs delegated (scoped token exchange)
Intersection rule: effective authority = agent's configured permissions ∩ user's current permissions
Token exchange via RFC 8693 produces downscoped token with user identity + agent scope + audience binding
Permissions evaluated in real time per tool call, not cached at invocation
Confused deputy defense: intersection rule limits blast radius of prompt injection via MCP

competitors.title: Securing agentic apps: Give your AI agents their own credentials (WorkOS Blog, Apr 6, 2026)
key_points: Three anti-patterns: borrowing user's session, shared service accounts, static API keys with no scoping
Agents as first-class principals — every action answers: who is acting, what are they authorized to do, can we prove it later
User-authorized agents use Authorization Code with PKCE; M2M agents use Client Credentials flow
RBAC at the tool level: each tool mapped to a required permission, default-deny for unknown tools
Fine-grained authorization (FGA/ReBAC) for resource-level control — agent can read marketing docs but not HR docs
Delegation chains: when agents call other agents, identity and scope must propagate through the chain

competitors.title: The security risks specific to MCP servers (WorkOS Blog, Jun 2, 2026)
key_points: MCP servers have different attack surface than traditional APIs — five key risks grounded in OWASP agentic AI guidelines
MCP authorization spec mandates OAuth 2.1 with scoped tokens for every tool invocation
WorkOS MCP Auth provides OAuth 2.1 and OIDC built in for MCP server authentication

competitors.title: How to manage API keys, tokens, and secrets for AI agents (WorkOS Blog, Jun 10, 2026)
key_points: Encrypted storage, OAuth connection management, and session-scoped access for autonomous agents
Credential gateway pattern: agent never sees OAuth tokens — requests backend to act on its behalf
Refresh tokens rotated on use, stored server-side only, expire if unused

angles: Auth is not a layer — it runs through all five layers of the agent stack, and getting it wrong at any layer breaks the system
The intersection rule: agent permissions must be the strict intersection of agent role and user permissions, never the union — this is the single most important security concept for production agents
Session-scoped authorization: agents get access for task duration only, not indefinitely — solves the long-lived token problem without replacing OAuth
Agent as principal: the industry is converging on treating agents as first-class actors with their own identity, not extensions of the humans who invoked them
MCP is the convergence point: it standardizes tool exposure, auth, and audit across the agent ecosystem — replacing the fragmented plugin/action/function landscape
Skills are the next abstraction layer: composable, versioned, shareable capability bundles that turn agents from single-purpose scripts into runtime platforms
The confused deputy problem: why intersection rule + MCP scoped tokens together neutralize prompt injection's blast radius
Fail closed vs fail open: authorization failures must be definitive stops — agents should never retry with different credentials or fall back to broader access
outline: Introduction: Why the vocabulary around AI agents keeps resetting — and why a clear stack map matters
The Five-Layer Agent Stack: A production agent is five concerns, not one script
Layer 1: User/App Surface — where humans enter the loop, HITL design patterns, async architecture for approval flows
Layer 2: Agent Framework — orchestrator (decision loop), memory (short-term context vs long-term external), system prompt (job description), skills (composable capability bundles)

Layer 3: Tools, MCP Servers, and Skills — what a tool actually is (function with JSON schema), what MCP solves (operational complexity, versioning, sharing), what skills are (packaged tool + prompt + context)
Layer 4: LLM/Model — where reasoning happens, prompt injection as OWASP's top threat, architectural mitigations (treat tool results as untrusted)
Layer 5: Auth and Identity — AuthN (who are you), AuthZ (what can you do), agent as principal, session-scoped access, audit trail
The Intersection Rule: Why delegated access alone is not enough — agent role ∩ user permissions as the effective authority
Token Architecture: Short-lived audience-bound tokens, RFC 8693 token exchange, DPoP sender-constraining, vaulted credentials
MCP Security: OAuth 2.1 with PKCE as the standard, scoped tokens per tool invocation, confused deputy defense
Skills and the Future: Skill marketplaces, composable agent capabilities, the agent as runtime platform
Audit and Attribution: Five questions every log entry must answer, immutable audit trails for enterprise compliance
Implementation Checklist: Per-agent identity, intersection rule enforcement, fail-closed design, immediate revocation
Conclusion: Auth is not a feature you add at the end — it touches every layer, and retrofitting is significantly harder than getting it right from the start
